HI Mark,

I forget if JAGS innately recognized pi as pi, but it needs to be specified (in the data or constants statement) in nimble. Making this change gets the toy example to function correctly.

PI = pi
# Build the model
model <- nimbleModel(code,
                     constants = list(n = nrow(v_data), pi = PI),
                     data = list(y = v_data),
                     inits = inits)

> model$var # I get all NAs here
 [1] 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808 0.2098808
> model$cov_matrix[1,,] # diagonal NAs here
          [,1]      [,2]
[1,] 0.2098808 0.0000000
[2,] 0.0000000 0.2098808
> model$calculate()
[1] -17.85664

Best,
-Dan

messages.subject: new nimble user: long computation time for simple model
messages.subject_clean: new nimble user: long computation time for simple model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm new to using nimble and trying to work through a simple process model that I wrote to get familiar with the package.

This is essentially an occupancy/sdm process model with counts of salamanders as the response and two covariates (temperature and precipitation). No spatial autocorrelation has been accounted for yet.

Y is a vector of counts of salamanders summarized to hexbin i with each row representing a different hexbin (810,707 rows)

X is a matrix with an intercept column, a temperature column, and a precipitation column. Temperature and precipitation are also summarized to hexbin i with the same number of rows as Y.

Some other notes:
-Y is over-dispersed and a negative binomial distribution should probably be used.
-Precipitation has a far larger mean and standard deviation than temperature. I've considered scaling but haven't attempted this yet because I need to figure out how this will impact my priors.

This model takes a very long time to run, and I'm unsure what the major cause of it is. I've tried reducing the sd of my betas and reducing the number of iterations just to get some sort of output but it hasn't stopped running after several hours. Is this just because I have a lot of rows or maybe it's having trouble converging without the observation model and spatial autocorrelation component? Please let me know if anything stands out in my code. Thanks!

data <- list(
    Y = Y, #a vector
    X = X #a matrix
    #spatial autocorrelation (ai) here
)

constants <- list(nbin = length(Y))

inits <- list(
  list(beta0 = 0, beta1 = 0, beta2 = 0.1),  # Initial values for chain 1
  list(beta0 = 1, beta1 = 1, beta2 = 1),        # Initial values for chain 2
  list(beta0 = 10, beta1 = 10, beta2 = 10)      # Initial values for chain 3
)#initial values cant all start at zero since they'll be logged?

monitors<- c("beta0","beta1","beta2") #what variables to monitor, didn't work will need to try this again

nburnin<-10 #mess around with this

niter<-100 #increase over time, was initially a lot higher

nchains<-3

code <- nimbleCode( {

# Priors
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd= 10) # Regression intercept
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd= 10) #Beta 1 temperature
    beta2 ~ dgamma(1^2/10^2, 1/10^2) #Beta 2 rainfall (rainfall can only be positive so we use a gamma here)

for (i in 1:nbin){

# Functions

  #Deterministic process model
    log(lambda[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * X[i,2]+ beta2 * X[i,3] #Function for intensity and log link

  # Likelihood for Process Model (Abiotic)

    #Intensity
      Y[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i]) #no inclusion of an observation model, modeling data directly here

    }
  }
)

#Simpler Nimble Model
processMod1<-nimbleMCMC(code = code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits, niter=niter, nburnin=nburnin, nchains=nchains, check=T, progressBar=T, samplesAsCodaMCMC=T, summary=T, WAIC=T)

messages.subject: Non-homogeneous Poisson Process with thinning method
messages.subject_clean: Non-homogeneous Poisson Process with thinning method
messages.body_plain:
Hello NIMBLE users,

I am currently working on fitting a non-homogeneous Poisson process using a thinning method to account for covariate impact on the event rate (lambda). However, I am struggling with data formatting, as I have continuous-time data (the time of events for several repetitions, e.g. the time of bus arrivals at several bus stops).

I can store them within a nimbleList (see the code below), but I'm not sure whether I can use this format for model data. I do not have a maximum number of events per repetition, so I cannot really preallocate the length of the vectors, or turn this into a matrix. And I cannot really use a summary variable (e.g. the number of events per repetition), because it would probably not fit well to what I'm trying to fit. I'm new-ish to using bayesian inference and Nimble, so maybe I've missed an obvious solution here.

Here is a reproducible example to illustrate my issue, including a base R data simulation and an unfinished draft of my NIMBLE model code:

```R
library(nimble)
set.seed(123)

# Link between my covariate and lambda (the event rate)
nimCompute_lambda <- nimble::nimbleFunction(
  run = function(lambda_intercept = double(0),
                 my_covariate_coef = double(0),
                 my_covariate = double(1)) {
    return(lambda_intercept + exp(my_covariate) * my_covariate_coef)
    returnType(double(1))
  }
)

# Define a nimble function for linear interpolation for a covariate depending on the time
nimCov_linear_interpolation <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(time_points = double(1), time_values = double(1), cov_values = double(1)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    nb_covariate_measures <- length(time_values)
    nb_time_points <- length(time_points)
    cov_interp <- numeric(nb_time_points)
    for (j in 1:nb_time_points) {
      time_point <- time_points[j]
      if (time_point <= time_values[1]) {
        cov_interp[j] <- cov_values[1]
      } else if (time_point >= time_values[nb_covariate_measures]) {
        cov_interp[j] <- cov_values[nb_covariate_measures]
      }
      for (i in 1:(nb_covariate_measures - 1)) {
        if (time_point >= time_values[i] & time_point <= time_values[i + 1]) {
          cov_interp[j] <- cov_values[i] +
            (time_point - time_values[i]) / (time_values[i + 1] - time_values[i]) *
            (cov_values[i + 1] - cov_values[i])
        }
      }
    }
    return(cov_interp)
  }
)

# Simulate data: the time of events --------------------------------------------
# With a non-homogeneous Poisson Process, using a thinning method
# (e.g. the time of buses arrivals at a bus stop and this depends on some covariate)

nb_repet <- 10 # Let's say I have 10 repetitions of this PP (e.g. 10 bus stops)

# Let's say I have covariate information every 2 hour for a day (so 13 covariate measures)
nb_covariate_measures <- 13
my_time <- seq(0, 24, length.out = nb_covariate_measures)

# I start by simulating covariates and the associated lambda
# (let's say here that I have only 1 covariate, and it's the same for every the bus stop)
my_covariate_values <- rnorm(nb_covariate_measures, mean = 0)
simul_lambda_intercept <- 0.1
simul_covariate_coef <- 1
my_lambda_values <- nimCompute_lambda(
  lambda_intercept = simul_lambda_intercept,
  my_covariate_coef = simul_covariate_coef,
  my_covariate = my_covariate_values
)

# The maximum lambda for oversampling events (with a margin, hence the * 1.1)
oversampling_lambda <- max(my_lambda_values) * 1.1

# I initialise my nimbleList to store the time of events
nimList_types <- vector("list", length = nb_repet)
for (i in 1:nb_repet) {
  nimList_types[[i]] <- nimble::nimbleType(name = as.character(i), type = "double", dim = 1)
}
nimList_def <- nimble::nimbleList(nimList_types)
nimList_data <- nimList_def$new()

# For each repetition, I'll run my non-homogeneous PP, and store the data in my nimbleList
for (i in 1:nb_repet) {
  # Homogeneous Poisson process with this oversampling_lambda
  oversampling_nb_events <- rpois(n = 1, lambda = oversampling_lambda)
  oversampling_event_time <- sort(runif(n = oversampling_nb_events, min = min(my_time), max = max(my_time)))
  # Association with a lambda: find the lambda at the time of events
  oversampling_expected_lambda <- nimCompute_lambda(
    lambda_intercept = simul_lambda_intercept,
    my_covariate_coef = simul_covariate_coef,
    my_covariate = nimCov_linear_interpolation(
      time_point = oversampling_event_time,
      time_values = my_time,
      cov_values = my_covariate_values
    )
  )
  # I get the ratio between the expected lambda and the max lambda (oversampling_lambda)
  oversampling_lambda_ratio <- oversampling_expected_lambda / oversampling_lambda
  # I make a Bernoulli draw for each point to see which points are kept
  oversampling_event_kept <- rbinom(n = oversampling_nb_events, size = 1, prob = oversampling_lambda_ratio)
  # I end up with those event times and store them in the nimbleList
  nimList_data[[as.character(i)]] <- oversampling_event_time[as.logical(oversampling_event_kept)]
}

nimList_data
# nimbleList object of type nfRefClass_52
# Field "1":
#   numeric(0)
# Field "2":
#   [1] 9.929384 9.949112
# Field "3":
#   [1] 10.61280 19.17420 20.58787
# Field "4":
#   [1] 6.585207 9.215271
# Field "5":
#   [1] 11.40760 17.04438
# Field "6":
#   [1]  4.201264  4.504587 15.762195 21.275257
# Field "7":
#   [1]  1.457294  3.415063  3.530273  9.856555 22.447195
# Field "8":
#   [1] 3.405766
# Field "9":
#   [1] 10.54636 18.87076
# Field "10":
#   numeric(0)

# Nimble model -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Now from this data, I'd like to estimate the link between lambda and my covariate.
# In other words, I want to estimate lambda_intercept and my_covariate_coef here.

my_nimble_code <- nimbleCode({
  # Priors
  lambda_intercept ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  my_covariate_coef ~ dnorm(1, sd = 1)

  # Compute lambda with my data
  my_lambda_values <- nimCompute_lambda(
    lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
    my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,
    my_covariate = my_covariate_values
  )

  # The maximum lambda for oversampling events (with a margin)
  oversampling_lambda <- max(my_lambda_values) * 1.1

  # For each repetition, I'll run my non-homogeneous PP
  for (i in 1:nb_repet) {
    # Homogeneous Poisson process with this oversampling_lambda
    oversampling_nb_events ~ dpois(lambda = oversampling_lambda)
    for (j in 1:oversampling_nb_events) {
      oversampling_event_time ~ dunif(min = min(my_time), max = max(my_time))
      # Association with a lambda: find the lambda at the time of this event
      oversampling_expected_lambda <- nimCompute_lambda(
        lambda_intercept = simul_lambda_intercept,
        my_covariate_coef = simul_covariate_coef,
        my_covariate = nimCov_linear_interpolation(
          time_point = oversampling_event_time,
          time_values = my_time,
          cov_values = my_covariate_values
        )
      )
      # I get the ratio between the expected lambda and the max lambda (oversampling_lambda)
      oversampling_lambda_ratio <- oversampling_expected_lambda / oversampling_lambda
      # I make a Bernoulli draw for each point to see which points are kept
      oversampling_event_kept ~ dbern(oversampling_lambda_ratio)
      # I keep this event only if I have 1 above. But how to use the nimbleList as my data here?
    }
  }
})
my_nimble_model <- nimbleModel(code = my_nimble_code)
```

messages.body_plain:
Hi Léa,

Thanks for the question. It looks like there may be some basics of nimble models that you'll need to get up and running here. When using a non-scalar in a model, you must always provide indexing brackets with an explicit index range (or a blank range if nimbleModel can figure it out from other parts of your model code or if you provide the dimensions argument, but I'd suggest explicit index ranges). For example, you would need:

my_lambda_values[1:N] <- nimCompute_lambda(

    lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
    my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,

    my_covariate = my_covariate_values[1:N]
  )

The second thing I notice is that you can't re-use variables in model code because it is a declarative language rather than (what most people are used to in most programming) and imperative language. For example, if you need a value of oversampling_nb_events for each i, you would need to do something like

oversampling_nb_events[i] ~ dpois(lambda = oversampling_lambda)

Each declaration (line of model code) creates one or more nodes (vertices) in the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the model. That's why you can't re-use a variable, A similar point applies to other declarations inside the for loops.

nimbleModel requires that you provide in the constants argument any constant values that are necessary to create a DAG representation from the model code. In this case, you would need to provide a constants list with at least nb_repet, oversampling_nb_events, and any values such as "N" that I gave above that you determine you need for vector or matrix index ranges.

A good way to build up a model when you are learning is to build it up piece by piece and see if it works at each step. For example, you could do only

my_nimble_code <- nimbleCode({
  # Priors
  lambda_intercept ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  my_covariate_coef ~ dnorm(1, sd = 1)

  # Compute lambda with my data

  my_lambda_values[1:N] <- nimCompute_lambda(

    lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
    my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,

    my_covariate = my_covariate_values[1:N]
  )
 })

my_nimble_model <- nimbleModel(code = my_nimble_code,
   constants = list(N = 10)) # not sure what N should be

# you will get warnings and/or NAs unless you provide inits for lambda_intercept and my_covariate_intercept or do calculate=FALSE.

my_nimble_model$lambda_intercept <- 0
my_nimble_model$my_covariate_coef <- 1 # not sure what values are reasonable
my_nimble_model$calculate()
my_nimble_model$my_lambda_values # are they what they should be?

You can also check that things will compile:
c_my_nimble_model <- compileNimble(my_nimble_model)
c_my_nimble_model$calculate()
# etc...

And then try adding in the next piece.

I'm not offering feedback on the model structure from a statistical perspective (that is usually beyond what we do here), so I am not seeing exactly what you want to do. In general, a nimbleList is not something you can use in model code (it is more for nimbleFunctions), and I am not clear how you were intending to use it. When people have subsets of data with different extents (what I think might be your need), a common scheme is nested indexing. For example, you could create a vector of data extents and use it like this

for(i in 1:nb_repeat) {
 #...
  for(j in 1:oversampling_nb_events[i]) {
   some_matrix[i, 1:length_of_data[j] ] <- some_function(<arguments>)
  }
}

You seem to have one data extent of 0 (but I may not be following) and that would be better to remove in advance.

It is also possible for a nimbleFunction with setup code to retain member data involving information about different extents for different indices. This is a relatively new feature and can be found in the user manual. I'm guessing you've had a look at the user manual (at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>) because of your exploration of nimbleLists. In case it is helpful, the early chapters on nimble models may be relevant to some of what you are running into.

HTH
Perry

messages.subject_clean: can't get nimIntegrate to work as expected
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the question.

integrand must be defined to take two arguments. Yours takes 6 arguments. The second argument should be a vector that you will need to unpack internally into the 5 pieces you need (i.e. to invert the way you packed them up as param=c(lambdasc,lambdaic,lambdafc, a, b), which makes sense).

The reason for the decreased flexibility of nimble's integrate (aka nimInterate) vs R's integrate is that it is not so easy in generated C++ (from compileNimble) to have functions of arbitrary numbers of arguments. (It could be done, but the current system is simpler than that.) So, instead, there is a single additional argument to nimIntegrate and the integrand function must be coded to unpack it internally. If you need lengths of components to unpack them (e.g. the lengths of a or b, which may not be determined easily when they are concatenated in a vector), you can include those lengths as elements in the vector as well.

I hope that helps. There is an attempt at explaining this in help(nimIntegrate). (integrate in a nimbleFunction becomes nimIntegrate.)

Perry

Hi Zhichen,

In model code (but not in nimbleFunction code), one must always use indexing brackets to indicate the number of index dimensions.

So please try replacing

rank_order <- all_permutations[m, ]

with

rank_order[1:N] <- all_permutations[m, ]

(where you will have to indicate what N is or use an appropriate constant for your case.)

I hope that helps.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
It looks like I missed that rank_order needs to be indexed by m as well, so it needs to be an array. But then that's what all_permutations seems to be. Now that I am looking at more of your model (beyond rank_order, which I specifically searched on last time because that was involved in the error message), it appears to me that your model code re-uses nodes. That is not allowed because it is a declarative model language (not an imperative language, as most programming is, i.e. sequences of steps). Each line of code declares a relationship among model nodes, so for example once a relationship for joint_prob is declared, it can't be re-declared as some different relationship. As it happens, a question from yesterday on nimble-users was about the same topic, so I will refer you to that: https://groups.google.com/u/3/g/nimble-users/c/unfd0Jtv7VI

messages.body_plain:
Hello NIMBLE community,

I have been using NIMBLE for my dissertation work and have enjoyed how user-friendly it is so far. I have come across a problem with where my posterior estimates from each of my 3 chains produce the same values. This problem occurs even when I specifically set different initial values for each chain. I'm not sure why this issue is happening and am looking for ways to try and troubleshoot or If anyone knows how to fix this issue.

For additional context, I am running a linear regression model with two explanatory variables. Please see my code below:

#IMPORT DATA
final <- read.csv("PLACES_FinalDataset_CityBoundaries.csv")

#SUBSET
final_PA <- final[final$StateAbbr == "PA",]

#NUMBER OF CENSUS TRACTS
N = as.numeric(dim(final_PA)[1])

#OUTCOME
smoke <- final_PA$smoke

#ICE MEASURE
ICE <-final_PA$ICEwbinc

#HOLC MEASURE
HOLC <- final_PA$HOLC_cnts2

#MODEL CODE
M0code<-nimbleCode(
  {
    #REGRESSION MODEL
    for(i in 1:N){

      smoke[ i ]  ~ dnorm( mu[ i ] , tau = tau.theta )

      mu[ i ] <- beta0 + beta1*ICE[i] + beta2*HOLC[i]

    }

    ######## PRIORS ########

    beta0 ~dnorm(0,0.001) #fixed intercept
    beta1 ~dnorm(0,0.001)
    beta2 ~dnorm(0,0.001)
    tau.theta ~dgamma(1,1/10) # regression precision

    #DEFINING REGRESSION VARIANCE
    sigma2.theta <- 1/tau.theta

  })

#INITIAL VALUES
init.vals<-list(
  #INITAL VALUES FOR CHAIN 1
  list(beta0=-5,
       beta1=-5,
       beta2=-5,
       tau.theta=0.1),

  #INITAL VALUES FOR CHAIN 2
  list(beta0=0,
       beta1=0,
       beta2=0,
       tau.theta=1),

  #INITAL VALUES FOR CHAIN 3
  list(beta0=1,
       beta1=1,
       beta2=1,
       tau.theta=3.5)
)

#CONSTANTS
constants<-list(N,ICE,HOLC)
names(constants)=c("N","ICE","HOLC")

#MODEL DATA
M0data<-list(smoke)
names(M0data)<-c('smoke')

#BUILD THE MODEL
M0<-nimbleModel(code=M0code,name="m1",constants=constants,
                data=M0data,inits=init.vals[[1]])

#COMPILE THE MODEL
CM0<-compileNimble(M0)

#MONITORS
M0Conf<-configureMCMC(M0,enableWAIC=TRUE,monitors=CM0$getNodeNames(stochOnly=TRUE,includeData=FALSE),print=TRUE)
M0Conf$addMonitors(c("beta0","beta1","beta2","tau.theta","sigma2.theta"))

#BUILD THE MCMC
M0MCMC<-buildMCMC(M0Conf)

#COMPILE THE MCMC
CM0MCMC<-compileNimble(M0MCMC,project=M0)

#RUN THE MCMC
updates <-runMCMC(CM0MCMC,
                  niter=100000,
                  nburnin=10000,
                  nchains=3,
                  thin=10,
                  inits = init.vals,
                  setSeed = 2468,
                  summary=TRUE,
                  samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE,
                  WAIC=TRUE)

I appreciate any help with this problem. Thank you.

Sincerely,

Ruby Bayliss

Backwards Indexing Warnings:

[Warning] Detected backwards indexing in '12:11'. This is likely unintended and will likely not produce valid model code.

I would appreciate any insights into why these errors may be occurring and how I can resolve them. I have attached the relevant model code for your reference.

Thank you for your assistance!

Best regards,

Motwaly

# write nimble model code
code <- nimbleCode({# intercepts
  for (s in 1:3) {
    phi_alpha[s] ~ dbeta(1, 1)
    p_alpha[s] ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  }

  # sex effects
  phi_beta ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  p_beta ~ dnorm(0, 1)

  # random effect SDs
  for (k in 1:2) {
    phi_sigma[k] ~ dexp(1)
    p_sigma[k] ~ dexp(1)
  }

  # random year effects
  for (t in 1:max(n_year)) {
    phi_year_z[t] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    phi_year[t] <- phi_year_z[t] * phi_sigma[2]
    p_year_z[t] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    p_year[t] <- p_year_z[t] * p_sigma[2]
  }

  # probability of transitioning to adulthood
  tau_alpha ~ dbeta(1, 1)

  # probability of being female for unobserved individuals
  pr_female ~ dbeta(5, 5)

  # open site loop
  for (m in 1:n_site) {

    # random site effects
    phi_site_z[m] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    phi_site[m] <- phi_site_z[m] * phi_sigma[1]
    p_site_z[m] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    p_site[m] <- p_site_z[m] * p_sigma[1]

    # open individual loop
    for (i in 1:n_ind[m]) {

      # sex (being female) imputation
      female[m, i] ~ dbern(pr_female)

      # open years loop
      for (t in first[m, i]:(n_year[m] - 1)) {

        # survival probabilities
        for (s in 1:3) {
          phi[s, m, i, t] <- expit(phi_alpha[s]                       # age-specific intercept
                                   + phi_beta * (female[m, i] - 0.5)  # sex effect (specified at -0.5, 0.5 for male/female)
                                   + phi_site[m]                      # random site effects
                                   + phi_year[t]                      # random year effects
          )
        } # s

        # transition probability
        # note: this is probabably a "nuisance parameter"; it doesn't tell you much, because a tortoise MUST transition to adulthood at some point which is more a function of its survival
        tau[m, i, t] <- tau_alpha  # intercept only

        # ecological process

        # departing state: <1 year
        ps[1, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                    # survives as <1, doesn't transition to juvenile (latter impossible)
        ps[1, m, i, t, 2] <- phi[1, m, i,t]       # survives as <1, MUST transition to juvenile!
        ps[1, m, i, t, 3] <- 0                    # survives as <1, transitions to adult (impossible)
        ps[1, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[1, m, i, t]  # doesn't survive as <1 (and thus didn't transition to juvenile)

        # departing state: juvenile
        ps[2, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                                     # transitions to <1 (impossible)
        ps[2, m, i, t, 2] <- phi[2, m, i, t] * (1 - tau[m, i, t])  # survives as juvenile, doesn't transition to adult
        ps[2, m, i, t, 3] <- phi[2, m, i, t] * tau[m, i, t]        # survives as juvenile, transitions to adult
        ps[2, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[2, m, i, t]                   # doesn't survive as juvenile

        # departing state: adult
        ps[3, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                    # transitions to <1 (impossible)
        ps[3, m, i, t, 2] <- 0                    # transitions to juvenile (impossible)
        ps[3, m, i, t, 3] <- phi[3, m, i, t]      # survives as adult
        ps[3, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[3, m, i, t]  # doesn't survive as adult

        # departing state: dead
        ps[4, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 4] <- 1

        # detection probabilities
        for (s in 1:3) {
          p[s, m, i, t] <- expit(p_alpha[s]
                                 + p_beta * (female[m, i] - 0.5)  # sex effect (specified at -0.5, 0.5 for male/female)
                                 + p_site[m]                      # random site effects
                                 + p_year[t]                      # random year effects
          )
        } # s

        # observation process
        # note: this can be inside of the same time loop

        # departing state: <1 year
        po[1, m, i, t, 1] <- p[1, m, i, t]
        po[1, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[1, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[1, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[1, m, i, t]

        # departing state: juvenile
        po[2, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[2, m, i, t, 2] <- p[2, m, i, t]
        po[2, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[2, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[2, m, i, t]

        # departing state: adult
        po[3, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[3, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[3, m, i, t, 3] <- p[3, m, i, t]
        po[3, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[3, m, i, t]

        # departing state: dead
        po[4, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 4] <- 1

      } # t

      # likelihood

      for (t in (first[m, i] + 1):n_year[m]) {

        # ecological process
        z[m, i, t] ~ dcat(ps[z[m, i, t - 1], m, i, t - 1, 1:4])

        # observation process
        y[m, i, t] ~ dcat(po[z[m, i, t], m, i, t - 1, 1:4])

      } # t
    } # i

    # derived quantities

    # site- and age-specific survival and recapture
    phi_m[m, 1:3] <- expit(phi_alpha[1:3] + phi_site[m])
    p_m[m, 1:3] <- expit(p_alpha[1:3] + p_site[m])

    # site- and sex-specific survival and recapture
    phi_female[m] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + phi_site[m] + phi_beta * 0.5)
    phi_male[m] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + phi_site[m] + phi_beta * -0.5)
    p_female[m] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + p_site[m] + p_beta * 0.5)
    p_male[m] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + p_site[m] + p_beta * -0.5)

  } # m

  # year-specific survival and recapture for adults
  for (t in 1:(max(n_year) - 1)) {
    phi_t[t] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + mean(phi_site[1:n_site]) + phi_year[t])
    p_t[t] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + mean(p_site[1:n_site]) + p_year[t])
  }

})

      female[m, i] ~ dbern(pr_female)

      # open years loop
      for (t in first[m, i]:(n_year[m] - 1)) {

        # survival probabilities
        for (s in 1:3) {
          phi[s, m, i, t] <- expit(phi_alpha[s]                       # age-specific intercept
                                   + phi_beta * (female[m, i] - 0.5)  # sex effect (specified at -0.5, 0.5 for male/female)
                                   + phi_site[m]                      # random site effects
                                   + phi_year[t]                      # random year effects
          )
        } # s

        # transition probability
        # note: this is probabably a "nuisance parameter"; it doesn't tell you much, because a tortoise MUST transition to adulthood at some point which is more a function of its survival
        tau[m, i, t] <- tau_alpha  # intercept only

        # ecological process

        # departing state: <1 year
        ps[1, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                    # survives as <1, doesn't transition to juvenile (latter impossible)
        ps[1, m, i, t, 2] <- phi[1, m, i,t]       # survives as <1, MUST transition to juvenile!
        ps[1, m, i, t, 3] <- 0                    # survives as <1, transitions to adult (impossible)
        ps[1, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[1, m, i, t]  # doesn't survive as <1 (and thus didn't transition to juvenile)

        # departing state: juvenile
        ps[2, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                                     # transitions to <1 (impossible)
        ps[2, m, i, t, 2] <- phi[2, m, i, t] * (1 - tau[m, i, t])  # survives as juvenile, doesn't transition to adult
        ps[2, m, i, t, 3] <- phi[2, m, i, t] * tau[m, i, t]        # survives as juvenile, transitions to adult
        ps[2, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[2, m, i, t]                   # doesn't survive as juvenile

        # departing state: adult
        ps[3, m, i, t, 1] <- 0                    # transitions to <1 (impossible)
        ps[3, m, i, t, 2] <- 0                    # transitions to juvenile (impossible)
        ps[3, m, i, t, 3] <- phi[3, m, i, t]      # survives as adult
        ps[3, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - phi[3, m, i, t]  # doesn't survive as adult

        # departing state: dead
        ps[4, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        ps[4, m, i, t, 4] <- 1

        # detection probabilities
        for (s in 1:3) {
          p[s, m, i, t] <- expit(p_alpha[s]
                                 + p_beta * (female[m, i] - 0.5)  # sex effect (specified at -0.5, 0.5 for male/female)
                                 + p_site[m]                      # random site effects
                                 + p_year[t]                      # random year effects
          )
        } # s

        # observation process
        # note: this can be inside of the same time loop

        # departing state: <1 year
        po[1, m, i, t, 1] <- p[1, m, i, t]
        po[1, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[1, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[1, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[1, m, i, t]

        # departing state: juvenile
        po[2, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[2, m, i, t, 2] <- p[2, m, i, t]
        po[2, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[2, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[2, m, i, t]

        # departing state: adult
        po[3, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[3, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[3, m, i, t, 3] <- p[3, m, i, t]
        po[3, m, i, t, 4] <- 1 - p[3, m, i, t]

        # departing state: dead
        po[4, m, i, t, 1] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 2] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 3] <- 0
        po[4, m, i, t, 4] <- 1

      } # t

      # likelihood

      for (t in (first[m, i] + 1):n_year[m]) {

        # ecological process
        z[m, i, t] ~ dcat(ps[z[m, i, t - 1], m, i, t - 1, 1:4])

        # observation process
        y[m, i, t] ~ dcat(po[z[m, i, t], m, i, t - 1, 1:4])

      } # t
    } # i

    # derived quantities

    # site- and age-specific survival and recapture
    phi_m[m, 1:3] <- expit(phi_alpha[1:3] + phi_site[m])
    p_m[m, 1:3] <- expit(p_alpha[1:3] + p_site[m])

    # site- and sex-specific survival and recapture
    phi_female[m] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + phi_site[m] + phi_beta * 0.5)
    phi_male[m] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + phi_site[m] + phi_beta * -0.5)
    p_female[m] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + p_site[m] + p_beta * 0.5)
    p_male[m] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + p_site[m] + p_beta * -0.5)

  } # m

  # year-specific survival and recapture for adults
  for (t in 1:(max(n_year) - 1)) {
    phi_t[t] <- expit(phi_alpha[3] + mean(phi_site[1:n_site]) + phi_year[t])
    p_t[t] <- expit(p_alpha[3] + mean(p_site[1:n_site]) + p_year[t])
  }

})

# constants, data, initial values, and parameters to monitor
consts <- list(n_site = n_site,
               n_ind = n_ind,
               n_year = years$n_year,
               first = first) |>
  glimpse()
data <- list(y = ch,
             z = z_known,
             female = female) |>
  glimpse()
inits <- list(z = z_init) |>
  glimpse()

params <- c("alpha", "beta", "sigma", "site", "year", "m", "t", "female", "male")
mons <- c(str_c("phi_", params),
          str_c("p_", params),
          "tau_alpha",
          "pr_female")  # updated parameter name

# model
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, consts, data, inits, check = F, calculate = F)

Thank you for your assistance!

Best regards,

Motwaly

> Hi Léa,
>
> Thanks for the question. It looks like there may be some basics of nimble models that you'll need to get up and running here. When using a non-scalar in a model, you must always provide indexing brackets with an explicit index range (or a blank range if nimbleModel can figure it out from other parts of your model code or if you provide the dimensions argument, but I'd suggest explicit index ranges). For example, you would need:
>
> my_lambda_values[1:N] <- nimCompute_lambda(
>
>     lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
>     my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,
>     my_covariate = my_covariate_values[1:N]
>   )
>
> The second thing I notice is that you can't re-use variables in model code because it is a declarative language rather than (what most people are used to in most programming) and imperative language. For example, if you need a value of oversampling_nb_events for each i, you would need to do something like
>
> oversampling_nb_events[i] ~ dpois(lambda = oversampling_lambda)
>
> Each declaration (line of model code) creates one or more nodes (vertices) in the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the model. That's why you can't re-use a variable, A similar point applies to other declarations inside the for loops.
>
> nimbleModel requires that you provide in the constants argument any constant values that are necessary to create a DAG representation from the model code. In this case, you would need to provide a constants list with at least nb_repet, oversampling_nb_events, and any values such as "N" that I gave above that you determine you need for vector or matrix index ranges.

When people have subsets of data with different extents (what I think might be your need), a common scheme is nested indexing. messages.body_plain:
Hi Motwaly,

The warning is probably coming from this line in your model code:

```

for (t in first[m, i]:(n_year[m] - 1)) {

```

You'll want to check that  for all the {m,i} pairs that that indexing produces a valid, non-empty, increasing sequence given your values of `first` and `n_year`. As the warning suggests, I wouldn't proceed without tracking down what is going on.

As far as the note about `z` that is just there for the case the `z` is fixed and a data node or unknown parameter node, in which case it is best to provide it in constants to avoid nimble doing unnecessary calculations behind the scenes that result from nimble not knowing that `z` will never change. Usually an index would either be fixed in advance or an unknown parameter in the model. In your case, it's complicated because it appears you are specifying the `z`s as data, but then there are a few of them that don't appear on the left-hand side of a declaration (the first cases that are observed). Those are the ones that Nimble's checking is flagging because it thinks they could be specified in constants. It should be fine to proceed despite that note.

I haven't looked closely enough, but it might be possible to rewrite the model a bit so that the `z`'s that do not appear on the left-hand side of a declaration are declared in constants, but you'd need to separate them out as a separate variable that is not part of the `z` that are actually observations with a distribution specified for them. That would silence the note. But I don't think it will make much difference in this case in terms of computational efficiency.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Heather,

Yes, it should be the case that the sum of `n_psi[ss,t,1:(nState+1),q]` is always equal to `n_post[ss,t-1,q]`.  If it is not, then we cannot do a valid multinomial density calculation.

It sounds like you are fixing both `n_psi` and `n_post` in advance. Have you checked that for all values of `ss`, `t`, and `q` that the sum and the size are the same?

More generally in terms of debugging, in this case I would set up the model and then see if you can run `model$calculate('n_psi')`. If sum and size are not the same you should see the error message without even running the MCMC.

-chris

P.S. if you eventually have a model in which node(s) with a multinomial distribution are unknown and being sampled in the MCMC, make sure you have the most recent version of Nimble, as a few months ago, we re-instated our sampler for multinomial nodes. It had a long-standing bug, so we had taken it out a year ago.

messages.subject_clean: Problem with Posterior estimates from each chain produce the same estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ruby,

It looks like you are using the same seed for all the chains. Then since your model allows for use of all conjugate samplers, after a short initial period in which the initial values affect the samples, the samples then are identical between the chains. You would see this if you set `nburnin=0`, but if those initial samples are discarded as burnin, it looks like all of the samples are identical. I believe this is fundamental behavior when all conjugate samplers are used.

You'll have to modify your use of `runMCMC` to use different seeds (see `help(runMCMC)`).

I had not realized this would happen, so it's interesting to see this. I believe one could prove that this is the expected behavior based on probability theory (though I'm not sure if the actual conditional distributions involved play a role).

I'm making a note for us to think about whether `runMCMC` should enforce the use of different seeds for the different chains.

-Chris

Oh, I had thought from your email(s) that `n_psi` was fixed.

So I see that `n_post` is also unknown. If that's the case you'd need to somehow have a joint sampler that samples `n_post` and `n_psi`, since the sum of `n_psi` constrains `n_post` to a specific value. We don't have a built-in sampler in nimble that would handle that. It would probably involve figuring out what such a sampler would involve mathematically and then implementing it as a user-defined sampler.

I haven't looked through all the indexing in your model carefully, but the main point here is that if any `size` in a multinomial distribution is random and being sampled, it needs to be done jointly with the values specified by the multinomial density.

messages.body_plain:
Dear NIMBL's users,

I’m a bit puzzled as this model has been running smoothly for the past six months, so I’m unsure why I'm encountering this warning now. Therefore, I uninstalled NIMBLE version 1.2.0 and reverted to version 1.1.0. Interestingly, no warnings appeared when running the model in this older version. What could this indicate? I expected the newer update to enhance NIMBLE's accuracy.

Best,

Motwaly

On Fri, Oct 11, 2024 at 7:25 PM 'Chris Paciorek' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Hi Motwaly,
>
> The warning is probably coming from this line in your model code:
>
> ```
> for (t in first[m, i]:(n_year[m] - 1)) {
> ```
>
> You'll want to check that  for all the {m,i} pairs that that indexing produces a valid, non-empty, increasing sequence given your values of `first` and `n_year`. As the warning suggests, I wouldn't proceed without tracking down what is going on.
>
> As far as the note about `z` that is just there for the case the `z` is fixed and a data node or unknown parameter node, in which case it is best to provide it in constants to avoid nimble doing unnecessary calculations behind the scenes that result from nimble not knowing that `z` will never change. Usually an index would either be fixed in advance or an unknown parameter in the model. In your case, it's complicated because it appears you are specifying the `z`s as data, but then there are a few of them that don't appear on the left-hand side of a declaration (the first cases that are observed). Those are the ones that Nimble's checking is flagging because it thinks they could be specified in constants. It should be fine to proceed despite that note.
>
> I haven't looked closely enough, but it might be possible to rewrite the model a bit so that the `z`'s that do not appear on the left-hand side of a declaration are declared in constants, but you'd need to separate them out as a separate variable that is not part of the `z` that are actually observations with a distribution specified for them. That would silence the note. But I don't think it will make much difference in this case in terms of computational efficiency.
>
> -Chris
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Motwaly,

Yes, in version 1.2.0 we started warning about backward indexing. Nimble will generally not properly handle cases where the for loop has indexes such as `10:9`.

Now if everything was working before, this is just a warning, and you could ignore the warning.

However, I would be cautious. I suggest that you check the values of

```
for (t in first[m, i]:(n_year[m] - 1)) {
```

You'll want to check that  for all the {m,i} pairs that that indexing produces a valid, non-empty, increasing sequence given your values of `first` and `n_year`.

For example, I suspect there is a pair of {m,i} values for which `first[m, i]` equals 10 and `(n_year[m] - 1)` equals 9. (I.e., that the first time for the ith individual is too large relative to the number of possible times for that year.)

More generally, you can run `Rmodel$getNodeNames()` and check that the `z[m, i, t]` and `y[m, i, t]` nodes that you expect are all in the model.

-chris

I expected the newer update to enhance NIMBLE's accuracy.

> > You'll want to check that  for all the {m,i} pairs that that indexing produces a valid, non-empty, increasing sequence given your values of `first` and `n_year`. As the warning suggests, I wouldn't proceed without tracking down what is going on.
> >
> > As far as the note about `z` that is just there for the case the `z` is fixed and a data node or unknown parameter node, in which case it is best to provide it in constants to avoid nimble doing unnecessary calculations behind the scenes that result from nimble not knowing that `z` will never change. Usually an index would either be fixed in advance or an unknown parameter in the model. In your case, it's complicated because it appears you are specifying the `z`s as data, but then there are a few of them that don't appear on the left-hand side of a declaration (the first cases that are observed). Those are the ones that Nimble's checking is flagging because it thinks they could be specified in constants. It should be fine to proceed despite that note.
> >
> > I haven't looked closely enough, but it might be possible to rewrite the model a bit so that the `z`'s that do not appear on the left-hand side of a declaration are declared in constants, but you'd need to separate them out as a separate variable that is not part of the `z` that are actually observations with a distribution specified for them. > >

messages.subject: Fit multiple datasets on the same model (with Laplace approximation) without rebuilding and compiling the model object
messages.subject_clean: Fit multiple datasets on the same model (with Laplace approximation) without rebuilding and compiling the model object
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am looking to fit a specific model on a large number of simulated datasets. To ensure fast fitting on each dataset, I am using a Laplace approximation. However, I have not found a way to update the data and refit the model without having to rebuild the Laplace object using the `buildLaplace()` function and recompiling it each time. Is there a way to update the data and fit the model without this step?

See the example below.

Thanks for you help!

Hassen

```
library("nimble")

n     <- 1000
beta  <- 0.2
sigma <- 0.5
X  <- rnorm(n)
Y1 <- rnorm(n, beta*X, sigma) # dataset 1

model_code <- nimbleCode({
  # priors
  beta  ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
  sigma ~ dhalfflat()

  # likelihood
  for(i in 1:n) {
    Y[i] ~ dnorm(beta*X[i], sd = sigma)
  }
})

model <- nimbleModel(
  model_code,
  data      = list(Y = Y1),
  constants = list(n = n, X = X),
  inits = list(beta = 0, sigma = 1),
  buildDerivs = TRUE
)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

laplace   <- buildLaplace(model, c('beta','sigma'))
Claplace <- compileNimble(laplace, project = model)

MLE1 <- Claplace$findMLE(c(0, 1))
MLE1$par

#++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
## use new data with the same model

beta  <- -0.5
sigma <- 0.9
Y2    <- rnorm(n, beta*X, sigma) # dataset 2

Cmodel$Y <- Y2 # updating data

MLE2 <- Claplace$findMLE(c(0, 1)) #------> this does not work properly on the new data
MLE2$par
```

Hi all,

I'm a new NIMBLE user (coming from Stan) and am trying to reproduce one of the models from this paper <https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000910000012> (specifically model K-L3), which uses a Chinese Restaurant Process to cluster verbs into classes, based on the distribution estimated from a Dirichlet-multinomial model of how often each verb occurs in each of two alternating constructions. I believe I have constructed this model correctly and am using a small sample of data reported in the above paper to verify this, but unfortunately each time I run the MCMC sampling, the R session aborts. I have tried compiling the model and checking to ensure that I'm not getting infinite/NaN/NA values for the log probabilities, which is not the case. I have a hunch that it may be related to the initial values I set for the parameters, but I'm really at quite a loss and would appreciate any help, advice, or just a second set of eyes on my code in case I'm missing another problem.

Here's my model code:
k.l3_model <- nimbleCode({
  z[1:N] ~ dCRP(conc = gamma, size = N)

  for(c in 1:K) {
    lambda[c] ~ dexp(1.0)
    alpha[c] ~ dexp(lambda[c])
    mu[c] ~ dexp(1.0)

    mu_vec[c,1:2] <- rep(mu[c], times=2)

    beta[c,1:2] ~ ddirch(mu_vec[c,1:2])
  }

  for (i in 1:N) {
    ab[i,1:2] <- alpha[z[i]]*beta[z[i],1:2]
    theta[i,1:2] ~ ddirch(ab[i,1:2])
    y[i,1:2] ~ dmulti(prob=theta[i,1:2], size=n_i[i])
  }
})

Here are the data I'm using:
ptw_e0 <- tribble(
  # y = vector with form DOD, PD
  ~v, ~verb, ~dod, ~pd, ~y,
  1, "read", 1,  1, mvbind(1,1),
  2, "give", 2,  1, mvbind(2,1),
  3, "show", 2,  1, mvbind(2,1)
) %>% mutate(n_i = rowSums(across(c(dod, pd))))

                    K = 3,
                    gamma = 1)
exp2_data <- list(y = ptw_e0$y,
                  n_i = ptw_e0$n_i)

chain1.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain1.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain1.inits$lambda), 3)
chain1.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain1.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain1.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain1.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain1.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain1.inits$alpha[1]*chain1.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain2.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain2.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain2.inits$lambda), 3)
chain2.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain2.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain2.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain2.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain2.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain2.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain3.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain3.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain3.inits$lambda), 3)
chain3.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain3.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain3.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain3.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain3.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain3.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

chain4.inits <- list(lambda = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       mu = rep(rexp(n=1, rate=1), 3),
       z = rep(1, 3))
chain4.inits$alpha <- rep(rexp(n=1, rate=chain4.inits$lambda), 3)
chain4.inits$mu_vec <- matrix(rep(chain4.inits$mu[1], 6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
chain4.inits$beta <-  matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=rep(chain4.inits$mu[1], 2)), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)
chain4.inits$theta <- matrix(rep(brms::rdirichlet(n=1, alpha=chain4.inits$beta[1,]), 3), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow=TRUE)

exp2_inits <- c(chain1.inits, chain2.inits, chain3.inits, chain4.inits)

exp2_mod <- nimbleModel(code=k.l3_model, constants = exp2_consts, data = exp2_data, inits = exp2_inits)
compiledMod <- compileNimble(exp2_mod)

params.to.save <- c("z", "theta")

n.iter <- 10000
n.burnin <- 5000
n.chains <- 4

nimbleMCMC(model=compiledMod,
           monitors = params.to.save,
           nchains = n.chains,
           niter = n.iter,
           nburnin = n.burnin,
           summary = TRUE)

Thank you so much!

--
Brennan Gonering

Dear Nimble devs,

in calling nimbleModel() I'm getting the following error:

"dim(X) must have a positive length"

which I don't manage to pinpoint further.

I notice this is appearing in a limit case where some of the 'constants' or 'data' given to nimbleModel() are one-row matrices, for instance with dimensions [1,1:8] or even [1,1].

Before sending a minimal working example (the whole model is quite complex), I wanted to ask: Is it possible that nimbleModel() is internally simplifying them to vectors or scalars, even though in R they *do* have a 'dim' attribute?

I've also tried specifying all of these limit-case dimensions in the 'dimensions' argument, but that doesn't seem to help.

Cheers!
Luca

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brennan,

It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow.

The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.

The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.

I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.

I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.

Would you be up for installing nimble from GitHub from a new branch in which I've made these changes and seeing if it works for your use case(s)?

remotes::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "crp_underflow", subdir = "packages/nimble")

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone. I hope you are doing well.

I am trying to run an MCEM (Monte Carlo Expectation Maximization) algorithm in Nimble using the command buildMCEM. The data generating mechanism is based off of this reading: https://oliviergimenez.github.io/banana-book/hmmcapturerecapture.html#marginalization under section 3.6. It is, in essence, a capture-recapture ecological framework and I want to estimate the survival probability phi and the detection probability p in an HMM.

 I am using Windows,  and my R version is 4.4.1, and my Nimble version is 1.2.1. I am following this workflow to implement MCEM algorithm: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/pumpMCEM.html

 The code for the data generating process is:

set.seed(2022) # for reproducibility
nocc <- 5 # nb of winters or sampling occasions
nind <- 57 # nb of animals
p <- 0.6 # detection prob
phi <- 0.8 # survival prob
# Vector of initial states probabilities
delta <- c(1,0) # all individuals are alive in first winter
# Transition matrix
Gamma <- matrix(NA, 2, 2)
Gamma[1,1] <- phi      # Pr(alive t -> alive t+1)
Gamma[1,2] <- 1 - phi  # Pr(alive t -> dead t+1)
Gamma[2,1] <- 0        # Pr(dead t -> alive t+1)
Gamma[2,2] <- 1        # Pr(dead t -> dead t+1)

# Observation matrix

Omega <- matrix(NA, 2, 2)
Omega[1,1] <- 1 - p      # Pr(alive t -> non-detected t)
Omega[1,2] <- p          # Pr(alive t -> detected t)
Omega[2,1] <- 1          # Pr(dead t -> non-detected t)
Omega[2,2] <- 0          # Pr(dead t -> detected t)

# Matrix of states

z <- matrix(NA, nrow = nind, ncol = nocc)
y <- z
y[,1] <- 2 # all individuals are detected in first winter, as we condition on first detection

for (i in 1:nind){

  z[i,1] <- rcat(n = 1, prob = delta) # 1 for sure

  for (t in 2:nocc){

    # state at t given state at t-1

    z[i,t] <- rcat(n = 1, prob = Gamma[z[i,t-1],1:2])

    # observation at t given state at t

    y[i,t] <- rcat(n = 1, prob = Omega[z[i,t],1:2])

  }

}

y

y <- y - 1 # non-detection = 0, detection = 1

The NimbleCode is then as follows:

 hmmsurvival <- nimbleCode({
phi ~ dunif(0, 1) # prior survival
p ~ dunif(0, 1) # prior detection

  # likelihood

  delta[1] <- 1          # Pr(alive t = first) = 1

  delta[2] <- 0          # Pr(dead t = first) = 0

  gamma[1,1] <- phi      # Pr(alive t -> alive t+1)

  gamma[1,2] <- 1 - phi  # Pr(alive t -> dead t+1)

  gamma[2,1] <- 0        # Pr(dead t -> alive t+1)

  gamma[2,2] <- 1        # Pr(dead t -> dead t+1)

  omega[1,1] <- 1 - p    # Pr(alive t -> non-detected t)

  omega[1,2] <- p        # Pr(alive t -> detected t)

  omega[2,1] <- 1        # Pr(dead t -> non-detected t)

  omega[2,2] <- 0        # Pr(dead t -> detected t)

  for (i in 1:N){

    z[i,1] ~ dcat(delta[1:2])

    for (j in 2:T){

      z[i,j] ~ dcat(gamma[z[i,j-1], 1:2])

      y[i,j] ~ dcat(omega[z[i,j], 1:2])

    }

  }

})

Specification of the initial values:

 zinits <- y + 1 # non-detection -> alive

zinits[zinits == 2] <- 1 # dead -> alive

initialvalues <- function() list(phi = runif(1,0,1),

                                  p = runif(1,0,1),

                                  z = zinits)

initslist <- initialvalues()

Also, specifying the constants and data:

myconstants <- list(N = nrow(y), T = 5)

mydata <- list(y = y + 1)

Then, I proceed with running nimbleModel, and this works fine. I use buildDerivs = TRUE to enable automatic differentiation.

caprecap =  nimbleModel(code = hmmsurvival,

                                  data = mydata,

                                  inits = initslist,

                                  constants = myconstants,

                                  buildDerivs = TRUE)

So far, everything works.

But, the moment I try to compile the above, I get an error:

 compiledcaprecap = compileNimble(caprecap)

Error: Failed to create the shared library. Run 'printErrors()' to see the compilation errors.

I think my RTools is correctly working (I seem to recall somewhere it was saying to check this) and to test by running

 Sys.which("gcc")

Sys.which("g++")

Moreover, using this link: https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/OIKTI20OgMs, I found I could test whether the compiler is working properly using a simple setup as such:

foo <- nimbleFunction( run = function(x = double(1)) {return(sum(x)); returnType(double())})
cfoo <- compileNimble(foo)
cfoo(1:10)

And this works fine too.

I really do not know where to proceed.

When I run ‘printErrors()’, I get, among other things:

using C++ compiler: 'G__~1.EXE (GCC) 13.2.0'

In file included from P_4_hmmsurviva_MID_1.h:6,

                 from P_4_hmmsurviva_MID_1.cpp:7:

C:\Users\etien\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.4\nimble\include/nimble/NimArr.h: In instantiation of 'NimArr<nDim, T>& VecNimArr<ndim, T>::operator[](unsigned int) [with int ndim = 1; T = double]':

P_4_hmmsurviva_MID_1.cpp:38:12:   required from here

C:\Users\etien\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.4\nimble\include/nimble/NimArr.h:1862:35: warning: format '%i' expects argument of type 'int', but argument 3 has type 'std::vector<NimArr<1, double>, std::allocator<NimArr<1, double> > >::size_type' {aka 'long long unsigned int'} [-Wformat=]

 1862 |           "values.size() is only %i\n",

C:\Users\etien\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.4\nimble\include/nimble/NimArr.h: In instantiation of 'NimArr<nDim, T>& VecNimArr<ndim, T>::operator[](unsigned int) [with int ndim = 2; T = double]':

P_4_hmmsurviva_MID_1.cpp:41:14:   required from here

C:\Users\etien\AppData\Local\R\win-library\4.4\nimble\include/nimble/NimArr.h:1862:35: warning: format '%i' expects argument of type 'int', but argument 3 has type 'std::vector<NimArr<2, double>, std::allocator<NimArr<2, double> > >::size_type' {aka 'long long unsigned int'} [-Wformat=]

In file included from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/string:51,

                 from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/bits/locale_classes.h:40,

                 from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/bits/ios_base.h:41,

                 from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/ios:44,

                 from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/ostream:40,

                 from C:/rtools44/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/lib/gcc/x86_64-w64-mingw32.static.posix/13.2.0/include/c++/iostream:41,

                 from P_4_hmmsurviva_MID_1.cpp:6:

But I do not know how to interpret any of this output of errors.

Any help would be appreciated. Please do let me know if you require more information from my end.

All the best,

Etienne.

Hi Etienne,

This seems to be failing because of the derivative-building with discrete nodes in the model. Our AD system should allow such nodes, but somehow with the nested `dcat` nodes, there is a failure.
I will file an issue for us to look into this.

For now, if you want to use EM, you can leave out `buildDerivs = TRUE` and then follow the instructions in `help(buildMCEM)` to use MCEM without making use of automatic differentiation.

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear Léa,

Sorry your follow-up has sat unresponded for almost two weeks. We try but sometimes we have travel etc. (in my case).

The extent of a for loop range must be a constant (either a literal number or a variable provided in the constants list). It cannot be a model node such as oversampling_nb_events[i]. The reason is that the model code is processed as a declarative language, with each line of code (and for each iteration of a for loop) declaring relationships among variables. Those relationships are not dynamically re-determined each time the value of a variable (such as oversampling_nb_events[i]) changes.

In such a situation, it is usually possible to define the model for the maximal needed range and then write code that achieves using only a part of the range in a dynamic way. I'm sorry I'm not seeing exactly what you need (your explanation refers to variables that seem to be in your first message, but there were other issues going on there and I'm not clear if the names are consistent or of exactly what you need). Would it be possible to now make a toy example with all the pieces you want?

Please refer to section 12.3 of the nimble User Manual for the idea I mentioned previously. It's a new section of the manual, so I hope it is clear enough.

I was able to run your code by editing it to use the values shown behind comment tags (#). It works really well if you are able to send minimal reproducible examples that run without any guesswork at all about how we should change what you sent such as uncommenting pieces of it. Thank you!

Perry

> > Hi Léa,
> >
> > Thanks for the question. It looks like there may be some basics of nimble models that you'll need to get up and running here. When using a non-scalar in a model, you must always provide indexing brackets with an explicit index range (or a blank range if nimbleModel can figure it out from other parts of your model code or if you provide the dimensions argument, but I'd suggest explicit index ranges). For example, you would need:
> >
> > my_lambda_values[1:N] <- nimCompute_lambda(
> >
> >     lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
> >     my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,
> >     my_covariate = my_covariate_values[1:N]
> >   )
> >
> > The second thing I notice is that you can't re-use variables in model code because it is a declarative language rather than (what most people are used to in most programming) and imperative language. For example, if you need a value of oversampling_nb_events for each i, you would need to do something like
> >
> > oversampling_nb_events[i] ~ dpois(lambda = oversampling_lambda)
> >
> > Each declaration (line of model code) creates one or more nodes (vertices) in the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the model. That's why you can't re-use a variable, A similar point applies to other declarations inside the for loops.
> >
> > nimbleModel requires that you provide in the constants argument any constant values that are necessary to create a DAG representation from the model code. In this case, you would need to provide a constants list with at least nb_repet, oversampling_nb_events, and any values such as "N" that I gave above that you determine you need for vector or matrix index ranges.
> >
> > A good way to build up a model when you are learning is to build it up piece by piece and see if it works at each step. For example, you could do only
> >
> > my_nimble_code <- nimbleCode({
> >   # Priors
> >   lambda_intercept ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
> >   my_covariate_coef ~ dnorm(1, sd = 1)
> >
> >   # Compute lambda with my data
> >   my_lambda_values[1:N] <- nimCompute_lambda(
> >
> >     lambda_intercept = lambda_intercept,
> >     my_covariate_coef = my_covariate_coef,
> >     my_covariate = my_covariate_values[1:N]
> >   )
> >  })
> >

> >    constants = list(N = 10)) # not sure what N should be
> >
> > # you will get warnings and/or NAs unless you provide inits for lambda_intercept and my_covariate_intercept or do calculate=FALSE.
> >
> > my_nimble_model$lambda_intercept <- 0
> > my_nimble_model$my_covariate_coef <- 1 # not sure what values are reasonable

> > my_nimble_model$my_lambda_values # are they what they should be?

> >

In general, a nimbleList is not something you can use in model code (it is more for nimbleFunctions), and I am not clear how you were intending to use it. When people have subsets of data with different extents (what I think might be your need), a common scheme is nested indexing. For example, you could create a vector of data extents and use it like this
> >
> > for(i in 1:nb_repeat) {
> >  #...

This is a relatively new feature and can be found in the user manual. > Hi Brennan,
>
> It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow.
>
> The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.
>
> The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.
>
> I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.
>
> I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.
>
> Would you be up for installing nimble from GitHub from a new branch in which I've made these changes and seeing if it works for your use case(s)?
>
> remotes::install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "crp_underflow", subdir = "packages/nimble")

> > Hi Brennan,
> >
> > It looks like this is occurring because, for the model structure and small dataset in the example, it's possible to get values in the theta and beta vectors that are exactly 0 from numerical underflow.
> >
> > The zero values in `theta` tend to happen when the `ab` values are much smaller than 1. The values of exact 0 cause the CRP sampling, which calculates the log probability density for a value of z conditional on theta, to have Infinity values when it tries to sample a new value of z, and that causes the error because we didn't anticipate the Infinity values could occur.
> >
> > The zero values in `beta` occur in the CRP sampling when attempting to create a new cluster by sampling from the prior for `beta`, and tend to happen when the `mu` values are much smaller than 1. The exact 0 value ends up causing a NaN value in the CRP sampling, which causes an error.
> >
> > I'm a bit surprised this hasn't come up before, but it may be that the size of the dataset and the specific priors combine to give a somewhat unusual situation.
> >
> > I've added a check that tries to handle the numerical issues more robustly, but I haven't tested it thoroughly yet.
> >
> > Would you be up for installing nimble from GitHub from a new branch in which I've made these changes and seeing if it works for your use case(s)?

Hi team,

Now I can use the NUTS sampler on continuous parameters (intercepts and slopes) while retaining other samplers on discrete parameters (in this case slice sampler on latent abundance) in N-mixture models (code attached). Everything looks great. For the same sample size and the same number of iterations, the NUTS sampler takes longer (72 seconds) than a MH sampler with block update (31 seconds), but the chains obviously are mixed much better for the former (attached). The only concern is that, even though it doesn't seem to cause any issues, I keep seeing this warning message when using the NUTS sampler (not for MH). I wonder if there is anything I can do to prevent this, or is it just fine?

Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'N[21]'. Current parameter value is 8.
Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'N[24]'. Current parameter value is 4.
Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'N[55]'. Current parameter value is 2.

BTW, I can only do this on my personal computer, and am still waiting for helps to make this happen on my work computer.

Best,
Qing

messages.body_plain:
Dear Qing,
Thanks for this report.
I believe things are working fine and the slice sampler is giving a false alarm. It is surprising that a case like this hasn't come up before. (Or, maybe it has but remained undiagnosed. Your small reproducible example is very helpful.)
Here is what I did (using N[53] as an example because that was among the last warning messages):
> compiled$model$y[53,]
[1] 3 1 2 1 2
> compiled$model$N[53]
[1] 3
> compiled$model$p[53,]
[1] 0.8414696 0.8484678 0.7847340 0.7212391 0.8531815
> compiled$model$lambda[53]
[1] 2.132799
> calcNodes <- model$getDependencies("N[53]")
> calcNodes
[1] "N[53]"    "y[53, 1]" "y[53, 2]" "y[53, 3]" "y[53, 4]" "y[53, 5]"
> Nvec <- 0:10
> lp <- numeric(11)
> for(i in 1:11) {
+ compiled$model$N[53] <- Nvec[i]
+ lp[i] <- compiled$model$calculate(calcNodes)
+ }
> lp
 [1]      -Inf      -Inf      -Inf  -8.85227 -14.59378 -21.52216 -29.14837
 [8] -37.25659 -45.72677 -54.48351 -63.47558
>
So we can see that the shape of the conditional distribution for N[53] has a mode at 3 and decreases for each higher integer value. That makes sense (i.e. it is a plausible situation). I believe this can trigger the slice sampler warning because it goes through a scheme where first it steps out to the left and right of the current value (which in this case is also 3) and then makes draws, stepping in if it doesn't get a draw that falls within the slice (as determined by a randomly drawn auxiliary probability level for the slice). In this case this will result stepping in endlessly to 3-epsilon and 3+epsilon, if the slice level is such that only 3 is a valid next value for the node. Sorry, I know this explanation will only make sense if you know how the slice sampling works. Anyway, I am going to test a fix to catch this situation and then respond again if I make progress.
In the meantime, please note from help(samplers) that you can turn off the warnings with a control parameter maxContractionsWarning=FALSE. (Of course, you wouldn't want to do that without believing they are harmless.) There will still be some wasted computation until I can make a better fix (if I am seeing the situation correctly).
Thanks for the report.
Perry

In this case this will result stepping in endlessly to 3-epsilon and 3+epsilon, if the slice level is such that only 3 is a valid next value for the node. Sorry, I know this explanation will only make sense if you know how the slice sampling works. Anyway, I am going to test a fix to catch this situation and then respond again if I make progress.
> In the meantime, please note from help(samplers) that you can turn off the warnings with a control parameter maxContractionsWarning=FALSE. (Of course, you wouldn't want to do that without believing they are harmless.) There will still be some wasted computation until I can make a better fix (if I am seeing the situation correctly).

> Perry

messages.subject: Questions on Particle MCMC Methodology in nimbleSMC
messages.subject_clean: Questions on Particle MCMC Methodology in nimbleSMC
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble users and developers,

I hope this message finds you well. I have two questions regarding the use of Particle MCMC and the specific definitions of this algorithm as outlined in the nimbleSMC paper (https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v100i03).
Could you clarify the difference between Particle MCMC and particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (PMMH) as discussed in this paper (Chapter 3.6, pp. 11–13)? Additionally, which of these corresponds to the RW_PF_block sampler in the nimble package?
Am I correct in understanding that when using this methodology(maybe PMMH), there is no need to calculate or be concerned with the rhat value of latent variables? My interpretation is based on the statement in the paper, “If the latent states, x1:T​, are not needed as part of the PMMH output, the steps to track and record them can simply be skipped.” I will, of course, be checking the convergence of the top-level parameters, θ.

Thank you very much for your assistance and clarification.

Best regards,
Kei

Dear Kei,

PMMH is a specific case of the more general idea of PMCMC (similarly to how MH is a specific approach to MCMC).

Yes, the RW_PF_block sampler is using MH sampling for the non-state-space parameters, so that is PMMH.

Yes, the states are sampled from their conditional distribution and there should be no need to use convergence diagnostics for them.

Perry

messages.subject_clean: Confusing error output when compiling Nimble distribution
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jaume,

Your code runs without problems for me. I can do:

Ctest <- compileNimble(dmarocc)
Ctest(x = x, ivec = ivec, nint = nint, nstates = nstates, FR = FR, ps = ps, po = po, log = 1)
# answer matches: [1] -23.92458

The compiler output has a set of warnings (and these we don't try to silence because doing so could be different on each OS+compiler combination), but I don't see any errors.

It appears the problem is that your system is denying you access to the compiled DLL. The "inDL" is a function defined within the source code for "dyn.load", which is used to load the DLL after nimble has called the C++ compiler on your system. (See here <https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/69af5a3859b0a45432a01f118dbecf5d8831085b/src/library/base/R/dynload.R#L22>. ) I am wondering if this could possibly have to do with some kind of permissions issue on your system?

Are you able to run a basic nimble example on your system (e.g. from our r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> examples or from the user manual)?

If you are adventurous and want to stop nimble immediately before it tries to load your DLL, you can do,

nimble:::cppProjectClass$trace(loadSO, browser)

Then compileNimble will stop right at the single line of code in the loadSO method of the cppProjectClass class and (from what you will see) you can enter getSOName() to see exactly where the compiled DLL is on your system (if you don't already know). And you can see the dyn.load call used to load it and can try that manually to explore why you are getting "Access Denied."

For now I checked your code on Mac, not Windows.

HTH
Perry

messages.subject_clean: R session crashing when sampling model
messages.body_plain:
hi Brennan,

Thanks for the follow up and the additional testing.

It looks like there is another related, but distinct, numerical issue that can come up in this case. What I am seeing is that when one of the two `ab[i,1:2]` values gets close to zero, numerical underflow can cause a sampled value of `theta[i,1:2]` (from its conjugate Dirichlet distribution) to be exactly (1,0) (or (0,1)). Then if that `theta[i,1:2]` is the only member of its cluster, when the CRP sampling goes to sample a new value for `z[i]`, it's possible that the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]` under the other clusters are all -Inf. And using the non-conjugate CRP sampler to sample `alpha[i]` and `beta[i,1:2]` values for a new cluster will generally give values that also have -Inf for the log probability density value for `theta[i,1:2]`. At that point, the CRP sampler is trying to decide between the various possible new values for `z[i]` with all the log probabilities being -Inf and the crash occurs.

This is a tricky situation. We can of course (and will at a minimum in our upcoming release) error trap this and produce an error message rather than a crash.

However, I am not seeing a good way around the numerical problems. It's not clear to me there is a way to sample `z[i]` when `theta[i,1:2]` is (1,0) in a way that retains the validity of the MCMC sampling (i.e., I don't think sampling uniformly from the possible `z[i]` values is correct). And I don't see a reasonable way to avoid getting exact (1,0) values in the conjugate sampling of `theta[i,1:2]`.

For your case, one possible work-around (if you will generally have only two elements of theta) is that you could specify theta[i] using a beta distribution and, as needed, use truncation to ensure it never is sampled as exactly 0 or 1:

theta[i] ~ T(dbeta(ab[i,1],ab[i,2]), .001, .999)

You could also think about using the stickbreaking representation rather than the CRP.  That might avoid the issue. Or it seems that in the paper you reference, they used some other sampling strategies based on drawing from the prior.

I will try to think more about this to see if there is a better numerical solution on our end.

-chris

> Dear Jaume,
>
> Your code runs without problems for me. I can do:
>
> Ctest <- compileNimble(dmarocc)
> Ctest(x = x, ivec = ivec, nint = nint, nstates = nstates, FR = FR, ps = ps, po = po, log = 1)
> # answer matches: [1] -23.92458
>
> The compiler output has a set of warnings (and these we don't try to silence because doing so could be different on each OS+compiler combination), but I don't see any errors.
>
> It appears the problem is that your system is denying you access to the compiled DLL. The "inDL" is a function defined within the source code for "dyn.load", which is used to load the DLL after nimble has called the C++ compiler on your system. (See here <https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/69af5a3859b0a45432a01f118dbecf5d8831085b/src/library/base/R/dynload.R#L22>. ) I am wondering if this could possibly have to do with some kind of permissions issue on your system?
>
> Are you able to run a basic nimble example on your system (e.g. from our r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org> examples or from the user manual)?
>
> If you are adventurous and want to stop nimble immediately before it tries to load your DLL, you can do,
>
> nimble:::cppProjectClass$trace(loadSO, browser)
>
> Then compileNimble will stop right at the single line of code in the loadSO method of the cppProjectClass class and (from what you will see) you can enter getSOName() to see exactly where the compiled DLL is on your system (if you don't already know). And you can see the dyn.load call used to load it and can try that manually to explore why you are getting "Access Denied."
>

>
> HTH
> Perry

Hi Thomas,

I haven't had time to look too deeply at this, but one initial thing that I see is that in the block of code below, the first two lines don't have `j` in them.  That leads to this warning:

```

Defining model

  [Warning] Multiple definitions for the same node.

            Did you forget indexing with 'i,j' on the left-hand side of

            `z_thetas[1:10, 1:7] <- thetas[z[i], 1:10, 1:7]`?

  [Warning] Multiple definitions for the same node.

            Did you forget indexing with 'i,j' on the left-hand side of

            `y_thetas[1:7] <- z_thetas[y[i], 1:7]`?

```

As a first step, could you rework your model so that you are not redefining the same node multiple times (i.e., defining `z_thetas[1:4, 1:7]` Q different times and similarly for `y_thetas[1:7]`). Once you've addressed that, let us know what happens in terms of the MCMC set up.

Also, these are minor side comments, but you don't need `setAlphas`. You can just set `alphas` via `constants` (or, it's also possible to do `alphas[1:7] <- rep(1,7)` though it's unnecessary here). And you don't need in the code to set `r[i, 1] <- i` . Just set that row of `r` via `data`.
